content: 1. Electric-powered wheelchairs have been studied for training purposes, with sensors being a key component of these investigations. A 2020 study (volume 20, issue 12, page 24) focused on non-wheelchair users. 2. Holden MK reviewed the use of virtual environments for motor rehabilitation in a 2005 publication in Cyberpsychology & Behavior (volume 8, issue 3, pages 187-211), including a discussion on overlapping studies. 3. Huang HH explored early power mobility training, motivation, and social participation in young children with motor disabilities in a 2017 article in Frontiers in Psychology (volume 8, article 2330), focusing on non-wheelchair users. 4. John NW, Pop SR, Day TW, Ritsos PD, and Headleand CJ implemented and validated a virtual environment for training powered wheelchair maneuvers in a 2018 study published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization & Computer Graphics (volume 24, issue 5, pages 1867-1878). This study did not involve wheelchair-specific training. 5. Johnsson C, Carlsson R, and Lagerstrom M evaluated training in patient handling and moving skills among hospital and home care personnel in a 2002 study in Ergonomics (volume 45, issue 12, pages 850-865). No relevant outcomes were reported. 6. Keeler L, Kirby RL, Parker K, McLean KD, and Hayden JA conducted a systematic review in 2019 on interventions promoting independent participation among community-dwelling middle-aged adults with long-term physical disabilities, published in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 14, issue 4, pages 391-409). Overlapping studies were noted. 7. Kehrer AL, Barkocy B, Downs B, Rice S, Chen SW, and Stark S reviewed interventions to promote independent participation among middle-aged adults with physical disabilities in a 2021 systematic review in Disability & Rehabilitation (pages 1-12). Overlapping studies were identified. 8. Kenyon LK, Hostnik L, McElroy R, Peterson C, and Farris JP systematically reviewed power mobility training methods for children in a 2018 article in Paediatric Physical Therapy (volume 30, issue 1, pages 2-8). Overlapping studies were reported. 9. Kenyon LK, Schmitt J, Otieno S, and Cohen L surveyed providers of pediatric power wheelchairs in the USA in a 2020 study in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 15, issue 6, pages 708-717). No wheelchair-specific training was included. 10. Kirby RL, Brown BA, Connolly CM, McRae S, and Phillips PL examined stair-handling techniques for individuals with unilateral lower-limb amputations in a seated position in a 2009 study in Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (volume 90, issue 7, pages 1250-1253). No wheelchair-specific training was involved. 11. Kirby RL, Crawford KA, Smith C, Thompson KJ, and Sargeant JM conducted a randomized controlled trial in 2011 on a wheelchair workshop for medical students, published in American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (volume 90, issue 3, pages 197-206). No wheelchair-specific training was included. 12. Kirby RL and Doucette SP analyzed wheelchair services and outcomes in less-resourced settings in Kenya and the Philippines in a cross-sectional survey published in Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. Another paper by Bazant et al. (2017) was referenced. 13. Kirby RL, Smith C, Parker K, Han L, Theriault CJ, and Doucette SP surveyed occupational therapists in Nova Scotia regarding wheelchair-skills training for clients and caregivers in a 2020 study in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 15, issue 7, pages 773-780). No relevant outcomes were reported. 14. Kirby RL, Walker R, Smith C, Best K, Macleod DA, and Thompson K conducted a randomized controlled trial in 2009 on manual wheelchair-handling skills by caregivers using new and conventional rear anti-tip devices, published in Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (volume 90, issue 10, pages 1680-1684). No wheelchair-specific training was included. 15. Lam JF, Gosselin L, and Rushton PW systematically reviewed the use of virtual technology for wheelchair skills training in a 2018 article in Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (volume 99, issue 11, pages 2313-2341). No relevant outcomes were reported. 16. Linden MA, Whyatt C, Craig C, and Kerr C conducted a randomized controlled trial in 2013 on the efficacy of a powered wheelchair simulator for school-aged children, published in Rehabilitation Psychology (volume 58, issue 4, pages 405-411). Non-wheelchair users were included. 17. Martins FR, Naves ELM, Morère Y, and de Sá AAR preliminarily assessed a multimodal electric-powered wheelchair simulator for training activities of daily living in a 2021 study in Journal on Multimodal User Interfaces. No relevant outcomes were reported. 18. McSweeney E and Gowran RJ reviewed wheelchair service provision education and training in lowand lower-middle-income countries in a 2019 article in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 14, issue 1, pages 33-45). Overlapping studies were noted. 19. Morgan KA, Engsberg JR, and Gray DB explored important wheelchair skills for new manual wheelchair users from the perspectives of healthcare professionals and wheelchair users in a 2017 study in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 12, issue 1, pages 28-38). No relevant outcomes were reported. 20. Park JM and Jung HS studied the effects of a modified wheelchair skills program for hemiplegic clients in a 2019 article in Assistive Technology (pages 1-8). No control group post-test assessment was conducted. 21. Rice LA, Isaacs Z, Ousley C, and Sosnoff J investigated the feasibility of an intervention to manage fall risk in wheeled mobility device users with multiple sclerosis in a 2018 study in International Journal of MS Care (volume 20, issue 3, pages 121-128). No separate findings for wheelchair users were reported. 22. Rushton P and Daoust G compared university-course versus boot-camp approaches for wheelchair skills training for occupational therapy students in a 2019 article in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 14, issue 6, pages 595-601). No relevant outcomes were reported. 23. Sakakibara BM and Miller WHEELCHAIR examined the prevalence of low mobility and self-management self-efficacy in manual wheelchair users and its association with wheelchair skills in a 2015 study in Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (volume 96, issue 7, pages 1360-1363). No wheelchair-specific training was included. 24. Smith EM, Rismani S, Ben Mortenson W, Mihailidis A, and Miller WHEELCHAIR explored the clinical utility of shared-control teleoperation for powered wheelchair assessment and training in a 2019 article in American Journal of Occupational Therapy (volume 73, issue 6, article 7306205020p1-p11). No relevant outcomes were reported. 25. Toro-Hernández M, Alvarez L, Vargas-Chaparro M, and Goldberg M assessed final-year occupational therapy students' knowledge of basic manual wheelchair provision in Colombia in a 2020 article in Occupational Therapy International. No relevant outcomes were reported. 26. Toro ML, Bird E, Oyster M, Worobey L, Lain M, Bucior S, et al. developed a wheelchair maintenance training program and questionnaire for clinicians and wheelchair users in a 2017 study in Disability & Rehabilitation Assistive Technology (volume 12, issue 8, pages 843-851). No wheelchair-specific training was included. 27. Toro ML, Eke C, and Pearlman J evaluated the impact of the WHO 8-step wheelchair service provision model in less-resourced settings in a 2016 cohort study in BMC Health Services Research (volume 16, article 26). No relevant outcomes were reported. 28. Tu CJ, Liu L, Wang W, Du HP, Wang YM, Xu YB, et al. systematically reviewed the effectiveness and safety of wheelchair skills training programs in improving wheelchair skills capacity in a 2017 article in Clinical Rehabilitation (volume 31, issue 12, pages 1573-1582). Overlapping studies were noted. 29. Van Boxtel A and Gnewikow D used wheelchair activity as a learning experience for student nurses in a 1995 study in Rehabilitation Nursing (volume 20, issue 5, pages 265-273). No relevant outcomes were reported. 30. Wang YT, Limroongreungrat W, Chang LS, Ke X, Tsai LC, Chen YP, et al. investigated the use of immediate video feedback for ramp, wheelie, and curb wheelchair skill training for individuals with spinal cord injury in a 2015 study in Journal of Rehabilitation Research & Development (volume 52, issue 4, pages 421-430).
